blocks.text: At The Photographers’ Gallery in London, ‘Sanlé Sory: Colour Years’ reveals a lesser-known chapter in the Burkinabé photographer’s career, documenting changing identities, cultural expression and everyday life in post-independence Burkina Faso.

What can a portrait reveal about a society in transformation? In ‘Sanlé Sory: Colour Years’, The Photographers’ Gallery revisits the remarkable career of one of West Africa’s most prolific photographers, revealing how colour photography captured the evolving identities and aspirations of a generation.
Best known for his black-and-white portraits of Bobo-Dioulasso’s vibrant youth culture, Sanlé Sory began experimenting with colour photography in the mid-1980s at his Volta Photo studio.

The exhibition presents meticulously restored colour prints from his archive, alongside record covers featuring Volta Jazz, a band associated with Burkina Faso’s flourishing post-independence music scene.

From families and couples to traders and shopkeepers, Sory’s portraits document changing fashions, relationships, and everyday experiences in a society negotiating political transformation and cultural exchange.
Established in 1960, the year of Upper Volta’s independence, Volta Photo became a space where individuals could construct and express their identities in front of the camera.
Curated by Taous Dahmani, ‘Colour Years’ offers a perspective on Sory’s enduring photographic legacy, foregrounding the relationship between portraiture, self-representation and social change.
Through colour, fashion and personal expression, the exhibition celebrates the individuals who shaped the visual history of modern Burkina Faso.
This exhibition is on view at The Photographers’ Gallery in London until 21 February 2027.
